MODULE 1: 
Transactions Management, 
Concurrency and Recovery
PART 1- TRANSACTIONS
MS. ALVINA LOPES

Contents
❖ Transaction Concept 
❖ Transaction State 
❖ Implementation of Atomicity and Durability 
❖ Concurrent Executions 
❖ Serializability 
❖ Recoverability 
❖ Implementation of Isolation
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 2

Transaction Concept
❖ Transaction is a collection of operation that form a single logical unit.
❖ Transaction is a unit of program execution that access and possibly 
update various data items.
❖ Transaction is an event that occurs in the database.
❖ Transaction reads a value from the database or write a values to the 
database.
❖ Transaction also performs group of task.
❖ Eg., A bank employee transfers $5000 from B’s Account to X’s Account.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 3

Transaction Concept
❖ A transaction must see a consistent database.
❖ During transaction execution the database may be inconsistent.
❖ When the transaction is committed, the database must be 
consistent.
❖ Two main issues to deal with:
❖ Failures of various kinds, such as hardware failures and system 
crashes
❖ Concurrent execution of multiple transactions.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 4

Transaction Concept 
Key Points:
• Consistency: Consistency means database remains in a valid state before and 
after a transaction. 
• Integrity: Integrity means the accuracy and correctness of data stored in the 
database. It ensures that all data follows defined rules and constraints such as 
primary key, foreign key, and domain constraints. 
• Reliability: Reliability means the ability of the database system to function 
correctly even in the presence of failures such as system crashes, power 
failures, or errors.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 5

Basic Database Access Operations 
1. Read / Access Data (R)
It is the operation of reading data from 
the database.
Data is fetched from disk (database 
storage)
Stored temporarily in a memory 
variable
Used when we want to view or use data
Example:
Reading account balance from database
2. Write / Change Data (W)
It is the operation of updating data in the 
database.
Data is taken from memory variable
Written back to disk (database)
Used when we want to modify data
Example:
Updating balance after deposit
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 6

Basic Database Access Operations 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 7
4. Rollback
Rollback is a Transaction Control 
Language (TCL) command.
It undoes all changes made in a 
transaction
Restores the database to the previous 
state
Used when an error occurs or 
transaction fails
Marks unsuccessful completion of 
transaction
3. Commit
Commit is a Transaction Control 
Language (TCL) command.
It permanently saves all changes
made in a transaction 
After commit, changes cannot be 
undone
Marks successful completion of 
transaction

Transaction Concept Contd
Example (Bank Transaction)
A bank employee transfers ₹50 from Account B to Account X
This transaction includes:
Read balance of B 
Deduct ₹50 from B 
Read balance of X 
Add ₹50 to X 
All steps must happen together — otherwise it causes inconsistency.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 8

Example Contd
Transfer of 50₹ from Account A to Account B.
Initially A= 500₹, B= 800₹. 
This data is brought to RAM from Hard Disk.
 R(A) -- 500 // Accessed from RAM.
 A = A-50 // Deducting 50₹ from A.
 W(A)--450 // Updated in RAM.
 R(B) -- 800 // Accessed from RAM.
 B=B+50 // 50₹ is added to B's Account.
 W(B) --850 // Updated in RAM.
commit // The data in RAM is taken back to Hard Disk.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 9

Stages of Transaction
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 10

Transaction Concept (CONTD)
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 11
• The database starts in a consistent 
state before the transaction 
begins.
• During execution, it may become 
temporarily inconsistent.
• All operations are performed 
within the transaction.
• After completion (COMMIT), the 
database returns to a consistent 
state.

Transaction State Diagram
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 12
Success path:
Active → Partially Committed → Committed
Failure path:
Active → Failed → Aborted

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
Example :
Transfer ₹5000 from Account A to Account B
1. Active State
• Transaction is currently executing
• Performing operations like read/write
Example:
Read balance of A 
Deduct ₹5000 
Add ₹5000 to B 
Transaction is in progress
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 13

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
2. Partially Committed State
• All operations are executed
• But changes are not yet permanently saved
Example:
₹5000 deducted from A 
₹5000 added to B 
Waiting to execute COMMIT
Almost complete, but not final
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 14

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
3. Committed State
• Changes are permanently saved in database
• Transaction is successful
Example:
Money successfully transferred 
Data stored permanently 
Cannot be undone now
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 15

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
4. Failed State
• Transaction cannot continue
• Due to error, crash, or invalid operation
Example:
System crashes after deducting money from A 
Network failure occurs 
Transaction stops
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 16

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
5. Aborted State
• All changes are undone (ROLLBACK)
• Database returns to its state prior to the start of the transaction.
• Two options:
• restart the transaction – only if no internal logical error
• kill the transaction
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 17

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
5. Aborted State
Example:
₹5000 deducted from A is restored 
No money transferred 
No partial update remains
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 18

Transaction Property
❖To ensure integrity of data, the database system must ensure:
1. Atomicity
2. Consistency
3. Isolation and
4. Durability
❖ Also, known as ACID Properties.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 19

1.Atomicity
• A transaction should be atomic, meaning it is executed completely or not at all. 
• A transaction cannot be executed partially. 
• Either all operations of the transaction are properly reflected in the database or none are.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 20

2. Consistency
• Consistency ensures that the database remains in a valid state before and 
after a transaction. 
• A valid state follows all rules, constraints, and relationships (primary key, 
foreign key, etc.). 
• Execution of a transaction in isolation preserves the consistency of the 
database.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 21

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 22
• The diagram shows a transaction transferring ₹100 from account X to account Y.
• X is reduced by 100 and Y is increased by 100.
• The total balance (i.e 700) remains unchanged, maintaining consistency.

3. Isolation
• Isolation ensures that transactions execute independently without interfering with 
each other. 
• Changes made by one transaction are not visible to others until they are committed. 
• It ensures that concurrent transactions give the same result as serial execution. 
Example
Two users updating the same account:
One transaction should not see partial changes of another. Ensures correct and 
independent execution
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 23

Durability
• Durability ensures that once a transaction is committed, its changes are permanently 
stored in the database, even if a system crash or failure occurs.
• After a transaction commits, the data is written to non-volatile storage (disk). 
• Even if the system crashes immediately after commit, the database can recover the 
committed data using logs or backups. 
• No committed data will be lost. 
Example:
After transferring money from Account A to Account B:
The updated balances are saved on disk. 
Even if the system crashes right after commit, the transaction remains intact after 
recovery.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 24

ACID Properties- Example of Fund Transfer
• Transaction to transfer $50 from account A to account B: 
1. read(A) 
2. A := A – 50 
3. write(A) 
4. read(B) 
5. B := B + 50 
6. write(B)
• Consistency requirement – the sum of A and B is unchanged by the execution of the 
transaction.
• Atomicity requirement — if the transaction fails after step 3 and before step 6, the 
system should ensure that its updates are not reflected in the database, else an 
inconsistency will result.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 25

ACID Properties- Example of Fund Transfer
• Durability requirement — once the user has been notified that the transaction has 
completed (i.e., the transfer of the $50 has taken place), the updates to the database 
by the transaction must persist despite failures.
• Isolation requirement — if between steps 3 and 6, another transaction is allowed to 
access the partially updated database, it will see an inconsistent database (the sum A + 
B will be less than it should be).
• Can be ensured trivially by running transactions serially, that is one after the other. 
• However, executing multiple transactions concurrently has significant benefits, as we will see.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 26

Implementation of Atomicity and 
Durability
❖The recovery-management component of a database system implements the 
support for atomicity and durability.
❖The shadow-database scheme:
➢assume that only one transaction is active at a time.
➢a pointer called db_pointer always points to the current consistent copy of 
the database.
➢all updates are made on a shadow copy of the database, and db_pointer is 
made to point to the updated shadow copy only after the transaction 
reaches partial commit and all updated pages have been flushed to disk.
➢in case transaction fails, old consistent copy pointed to by db_pointer can 
be used, and the shadow copy can be deleted.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 27

Implementation of Atomicity and 
Durability
The shadow-database scheme:
• Assumes disks to not fail.
• Useful for text editors, but extremely inefficient for large databases: executing 
a single transaction requires copying the entire database.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 28

Concurrent Executions
❖ Multiple transactions are allowed to run concurrently in the system.
❖ Advantages are:
❖improved throughput and increased processor and disk utilization, leading 
to better transaction throughput: one transaction can be using the CPU 
while another is reading from or writing to the disk 
❖Reduced waiting time and reduced average response time for transactions: 
short transactions need not wait behind long ones.
❖ Concurrency control schemes – mechanisms to achieve isolation, i.e., to 
control the interaction among the concurrent transactions in order to prevent 
them from destroying the consistency of the database.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 29

Schedule
A schedule is an ordered sequence of operations (read, write, commit, etc.) from 
one or more transactions, representing how the transactions are executed in the 
database system.
Key Points
A schedule determines the execution order of operations from multiple 
transactions 
It can include: 
◦ Operations of a single transaction, or 
◦ Interleaved operations of multiple transactions 
It preserves the order of operations within each transaction
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 30
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 31

Serial Schedules in DBMS
❖A serial schedule is a schedule in which transactions are executed one after 
another, without any interleaving of operations.
❖Only one transaction executes at a time
❖The next transaction starts only after the previous one finishes
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 32

Serial Schedules in DBMS
Key Characteristics
Serial schedules are always:
Consistent
→ Database remains correct because there is no interference between 
transactions 
Recoverable
→ A transaction commits only after the transactions it depends on have 
committed 
Cascadeless
→ No transaction reads uncommitted data, so no cascading rollback
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 33

Serial Schedules in DBMS
Problems with Serial Scheduling
Although serial schedules are safe and simple, they have several performance 
drawbacks:
1. More Waiting Time
2. Less Resource Utilization
3. Less Throughput
4. Late Response Time
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 34

Examples of Serial Schedules
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 35

Non-Serial Schedule 
A non-serial schedule is a schedule in which multiple transactions execute 
concurrently, and their operations are interleaved (mixed) with each other.
Key Characteristics
Non-serial schedules are NOT always: Consistent, Recoverable, Cascadeless.
Advantages
Reduced Waiting Time: Transactions do not wait for others to complete 
Increased Resource Utilization: CPU, memory, and I/O are used efficiently 
Decreased Response Time: Faster execution for individual transactions 
Higher Throughput: More transactions completed per unit time 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 36

Examples of Non-Serial Schedules
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 37

Concurrent Executions
•Concurrent execution means that multiple transactions are executed 
simultaneously in an interleaved(one after other) manner, rather than one 
transaction completing before another begins.
•When multiple transactions execute concurrently without proper control, it 
may lead to problems affecting data integrity and consistency. Such issues are 
called Concurrency Problems (or Anomalies)
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 38

Concurrency Problems
1. Lost Update (Write–Write Conflict)
2. Uncommitted Data / Dirty Read (Write–Read Conflict)
3. Inconsistent Retrieval / Unrepeatable Read (Read–Write Conflict)
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 39

Concurrent Executions
Solution
To ensure correctness, DBMS enforces:
Serializability
Concurrent schedule must produce the same result as some serial schedule
Concurrency Control Techniques
•Locking (2PL – Two Phase Locking) 
•Timestamp Ordering 
•Validation-based protocols
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 40

Serializability
•Serializability is a concept in DBMS that ensures that even when transactions are 
executed concurrently (non-serially), the final result is equivalent to some serial 
(one-by-one) execution, thus maintaining a consistent database.
There are two ways to check whether any non-serial schedule is serializable.
1. Conflict Serializability
2. View Serializability
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 41

Types of Serializability
1. Conflict Serializability
A schedule is said to be conflict serializable if it can be converted into a serial 
schedule by swapping only non-conflicting operations, without changing the 
effect of the schedule.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 42

Types of Serializability
Conflict Serializability
Two operations conflict if:
• They belong to different transactions, and 
• They operate on the same data item, and 
• At least one of them is a write (W) operation.
Types of Conflicts
•Read–Write (R–W)
•Write–Read (W–R)
•Write–Write (W–W)
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 43

Precedence Graph (Serialization Graph)
A precedence graph is a directed graph used to determine whether a schedule is 
conflict serializable.
Steps to Check Conflict Serializability
Create Nodes
◦ For each transaction 𝑇𝑖
 ,create a node (vertex) in the graph 
Add Edges
◦ For every conflicting operation pair, draw a directed edge 𝑇𝑖 → 𝑇𝑗
if an operation of 𝑇𝑖 occurs before a conflicting operation of 𝑇𝑗
Check for Cycles
◦ No Cycle → Schedule is Conflict Serializable
◦ Cycle Present → Schedule is Not Conflict Serializable
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 44

Tj writes after Ti reads 
Write–Read (W–R)
Tj reads after Ti writes 
Write–Write (W–W)
Tj writes after Ti writes 
These rules come directly from conflict conditions

View Serializability
A schedule is said to be view serializable if it is view equivalent to some serial 
schedule.
View Equivalent Schedules
Two schedules (one serial and one non-serial) are said to be view equivalent if 
they satisfy the following conditions:
1. Initial Read: If a transaction reads the initial value of a data item in one 
schedule,
it must read the initial value in the other schedule also. 
2. Read-From Relationship: If a transaction reads a value written by another 
transaction, it must read from the same transaction in both schedules. 
3. Final Write: The last write operation on each data item must be done by the 
same transaction in both schedules.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 54

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 55
Two schedules S1 and S2 are view equivalent if:
1. Initial Read Condition
If a transaction reads the initial value of a data item in S1,
it must read the initial value in S2 also. 
2. Read-From Condition (Very Important )
If a transaction Ti reads a value written by Tj in S1,
then in S2 also, Ti must read from Tj
3. Final Write Condition
The last write on each data item must be done by the same transaction in both 
schedules. 
Schedules S1 and S2 are said to be view equivalent if they have the same initial reads, the 
same read-from relationships, and the same final write operations on all data items.

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 56
INITIAL READ
•In schedule S, transaction T1 performs R(A) before any write operation on A, so 
it reads the initial value of A. 
•However, in schedule S′, transaction T2 performs W(A) before T1 reads A, so T1 
reads the value written by T2 instead of the initial value. 
•This violates the initial read condition of view equivalence, which requires that 
a transaction must read the same initial value in both schedules. 
•Therefore, schedules S and S′ are not view equivalent.

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 57
Updated Read:
•In schedule S, transaction T2 writes the value of B, and then transaction T3 reads B, so T3 reads 
the value written by T2. 
•However, in schedule S′, the order of operations changes, but T3 still reads B after T2 writes it, 
meaning T3 reads the value written by T2 in both schedules. 
•Since the read-from relationship (i.e., which transaction writes and which transaction reads) is 
preserved in both schedules, the read-from condition is satisfied.
•Therefore, with respect to updated read (read-from condition), schedules S and S′ are view 
equivalent.

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 58
Final Write / Final Update
•In schedule S, transaction T1 first writes A, followed by T2 reading A, and finally transaction T3 
performs the last write on A. 
•In schedule S′, although the order of operations is different, the final write on data item A is still 
performed by transaction T3. 
•Since the final write on A is carried out by the same transaction (T3) in both schedules, the final 
write condition is satisfied. 
•Therefore, schedules S and S′ are view equivalent with respect to the final update condition.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 59

Shortcut Trick

This gives you the expected serial order
Step 2: Check Read-From Relation

Testing for View Serializability
Checking Whether a Schedule is View Serializable Or Not
Method-01: Check whether the given schedule is conflict serializable or not.
Method-02: Check if there exists any blind write operation.
Method-03: Try finding a view equivalent serial schedule.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 64

Testing for View Serializability
Method-01: Check whether the given schedule is conflict 
serializable or not.
❖If the given schedule is conflict serializable, then it is surely view 
serializable. Stop and report your answer.
❖If the given schedule is not conflict serializable, then it may or may not be 
view serializable. Go and check using other methods.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 65

Testing for View Serializability
Method-02: Check if there exists any blind write operation.
❖Writing without reading is called as a blind write.
❖If there does not exist any blind write, then the schedule is surely not view 
serializable. Stop and report your answer.
❖If there exists any blind write, then the schedule may or may not be view 
serializable. Go and check using other methods.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 66

Testing for View Serializability
Method-03: Try finding a view equivalent serial schedule.
3 conditions for view serializability: initial read, read from, final write.
❖By using the above three conditions, write all the dependencies.
❖Then, draw a graph using those dependencies.
❖If there exists no cycle in the graph, then the schedule is view serializable 
otherwise not.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 67

Serializability
❖A conflict serializable schedule is always view serializable . 
❖A view serializable schedule is not always conflict serializable . 
❖Conflict serializability is stricter, view serializability is more general.
❖Every view serializable schedule that is not conflict serializable has blind 
writes.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 68

Serializability
Advantages of Serializability
1. Predictable Execution 
2. Easier Debugging 
3. Lower Costs 
4. Better Performance 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 69

Recoverability
❖Need to address the effect of transaction failures on concurrently running transactions.
Recoverable schedule
❖If a transaction Tj reads a data items previously written by a transaction Ti , the commit 
operation of Ti appears before the commit operation of Tj. 
❖The following schedule is not recoverable if T9 commits immediately after the read.
❖If T8 should abort, T9 would have read (and possibly shown to the user) an inconsistent 
database state. Hence database must ensure that schedules are recoverable.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 70

Recoverability
Cascading rollback
❖A single transaction failure leads to a series of transaction rollbacks. 
❖Consider the following schedule where none of the transactions has yet committed (so 
the schedule is recoverable).
❖If T10 fails, T11 and T12 must also be rolled back.
❖Can lead to the undoing of a significant amount of work.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 71

Recoverability
Cascadeless schedules
❖Cascading rollbacks cannot occur.
❖For each pair of transactions Ti and Tj such that Tj reads a data item previously written 
by Ti, the commit operation of Ti appears before the read operation of Tj.
❖Every cascadeless schedule is also recoverable.
❖It is desirable to restrict the schedules to those that are cascadeless.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 72

Implementation of Isolation
❖Schedules must be conflict or view serializable, and recoverable, for the 
sake of database consistency, and preferably cascadeless. 
❖A policy in which only one transaction can execute at a time generates 
serial schedules, but provides a poor degree of concurrency. 
❖Concurrency-control schemes tradeoff between the amount of concurrency 
they allow and the amount of overhead that they incur.
❖Some schemes allow only conflict-serializable schedules to be generated.
❖Others allow view-serializable schedules that are not conflict-serializable.

Transaction management
Transaction management is the process of managing transactions in a 
database so that they are executed correctly, safely, and reliably.
Benefits:
• Concurrency Control
• Maintains ACID Properties
• Handles Read/Write Conflicts
• Ensures Recoverability
• Provides Serializability
• Controls Cascading Effects

TCL (Transaction Control Language)
TCL (Transaction Control Language) is a set of SQL commands used to control and 
manage transactions in a database.
TCL helps you:
• Save changes
• Undo changes
• Control how transactions behave
Main TCL Commands
1. COMMIT
2. ROLLBACK
3. SAVEPOINT
4. SET TRANSACTION
